query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high‐entropy alloys, the degree of chemical short‐range order (CSRO) within the nominally FCC matrix governs phase stability and simultaneously enhances high‐temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness by raising antiphase‐boundary energy to impede dislocation motion and by reducing point‐defect mobility.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni single‐phase FCC solid solution with minimal CSRO (as‐cast).
generation.intervention: Isothermal aging at 600–800 °C for 0–100 h to progressively increase CSRO without inducing long‐range B2 precipitation.
generation.conditions: Aging temperatures: 600–800 °C; mechanical tests at –196 °C and 800 °C; corrosion tests in 0.1 M H₂SO₄ at 25 °C; ion‐irradiation to 1 dpa at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of CSRO measured by diffuse scattering intensity at FCC {100} positions in XRD or by diffuse spots in TEM SAED.
generation.mechanism: Increased CSRO raises antiphase‐boundary energy, increasing CRSS for dislocation slip (strengthening at both cryogenic and elevated temperatures), and traps point defects (improving radiation tolerance) while reducing fast diffusion pathways (enhancing corrosion resistance).
generation.predicted_outcome: With increasing CSRO, yield strength at –196 °C and 800 °C will rise monotonically, corrosion current density in 0.1 M H₂SO₄ will decrease, and post-irradiation defect‐cluster density will diminish relative to the low‐CSRO baseline.
generation.baseline: As‐cast equiatomic alloy showing minimal CSRO (diffuse scattering intensity near background level).
generation.boundary: Applicable for Al contents up to ~10 at %, aging between 600 and 800 °C (CSRO below B2‐nucleation threshold), mechanical tests between –196 °C and 800 °C, radiation doses ≤1 dpa, and mild acidic corrosion environments.
generation.uncertainty: Exact CSRO threshold for onset of long‐range B2 ordering is unknown; quantitative relationships between CSRO magnitude and defect mobility/property metrics are imprecise.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two samples: (1) as‐cast low‐CSRO; (2) peak‐aged at 700 °C for 24 h high‐CSRO. Measure CSRO via XRD diffuse scattering. Perform tensile tests at –196 °C and 800 °C, corrosion tests in 0.1 M H₂SO₄ at 25 °C, and irradiate both to 1 dpa followed by TEM quantification of defect clusters.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high‐CSRO sample does not show both higher yield strengths, lower corrosion current, and reduced defect‐cluster density compared to the low‐CSRO baseline, or if long‐range B2 precipitation occurs at CSRO levels below those required for the predicted property changes, the hypothesis is falsified.
